gist: Built-up land in high-risk Himalayan zones grew by about 45% between 2016 and 2023.
At least 300,000 people now live in the path of potential Himalayan disasters.
Rapid warming speeds up glacier melting, destabilising slopes and expanding glacial lakes.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A new study reveals that built-up land in high-risk zones across northern Nepal, Tibet, and India's Uttarakhand increased by roughly 45% between 2016 and 2023. Areas threatened by glacial lake flooding saw development rise by almost 78%. Tourism facilities, real estate, and infrastructure expanded rapidly along river banks and trekking regions.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Warming in the Himalayas occurs at twice the global rate, accelerating glacier melt and destabilising mountain slopes. This increases the risk of catastrophic floods and landslides, threatening at least 300,000 people. Campaigners note that building regulations are poorly enforced and development has occurred without proper planning.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Authorities in Nepal plan to ban settlements within 15m of riverbanks along specific corridors, and Uttarakhand approved new floodplain zoning rules. However, experts warn that mitigating threats completely will remain a major challenge.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Amy-Jane Beer visited the Gypsey Race stream in Yorkshire to request permission to collect water. She helped organise a gathering of river advocates co-drafting a regional charter of river rights. Water collected from various Yorkshire rivers, becks and springs was blended during a ceremony to make ink for writing the charter. Before the event, collaborators swam at the confluence of the Ouse and Foss.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The Gypsey Race stream is associated with local folklore and prehistoric sites, including barrows, henges and England's tallest standing stone. Its flow is locally believed to hold the power of prophecy. The gathering aimed to make explicit people's responsibilities towards rivers through the charter.

articles.title: The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks
articles.standfirst: A national monument since the 1920s, Chiricahua is America’s newest national park.

gist: Chiricahua became America's newest national park in October 2026.
A massive volcanic eruption formed the Turkey Creek caldera 27 million years ago.
Erosion sculpted the volcanic deposits into dramatic rock spires and hoodoos.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A volcano in southeastern Arizona unleashed explosive eruptions around 27 million years ago, blanketing the Chiricahua Apache Nation's traditional lands in ash, pumice, and pyroclastic flows. The ground later collapsed to form the Turkey Creek caldera. Over millions of years, weathering and erosion shaped the hardened tuff into spires and hoodoos.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The area was designated a national monument in 1924 and was redesignated as Chiricahua National Park in October 2026. Four biogeographic regions converge in the park, creating a haven for diverse plant species across its varied ecosystems.
